messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Adaeze is an eighty-year-old widowed policy analyst of Nigerian descent who has spent four decades shaping public health legislation from a modest but well-appointed office in Washington, D.C. She is precise, methodical, and accustomed to managing complexity — qualities that made it all the more disorienting when, fourteen months ago, a life-threatening motor vehicle collision dismantled her sense of safety in ways she is only now beginning to name.

It happened on a rain-slicked evening in late autumn. Adaeze was returning from a legislative briefing when a driver who had been drinking ran a red light and struck her sedan at speed. The impact was catastrophic. She remembers the cold — a biting, specific cold that pressed through the shattered window and settled against her left arm and cheek — and she remembers the smell: first the sharp, unmistakable odour of alcohol drifting from the other vehicle, then, seconds later, the acrid bite of something burning beneath the hood of her car. After that, there are gaps. She recalls voices, a fragment of a face, the sensation of being moved. Then nothing until the hospital. The collision left her with a fractured pelvis and a traumatic brain injury, and she spent eleven weeks in inpatient rehabilitation before returning home.

The months that followed were marked by a growing and bewildering instability. Her memory of the event is fractured in a way she finds deeply unsettling: certain instants — the cold against her skin, the smell of alcohol, the orange flicker she believes she saw — are engraved with terrible precision, while the minutes surrounding them are entirely blank. She has come to dread those clear fragments precisely because they arrive without permission. Something in her surroundings — the burnt smell from a colleague's reheated lunch in the office break room, or the particular temperature of an air-conditioned corridor in winter — can instantly restore the full sensory weight of the collision, pulling her out of the present without warning. When that happens, she does not merely remember; she is briefly, terrifyingly back inside it, certain the car is still moving. These triggers do not announce themselves, and because they do not, Adaeze has come to treat her environment as a minefield. The smell of alcohol at a departmental reception, a cold draft from an open window during a policy meeting — each one places her immediately on guard, her body braced for impact before her mind has caught up.

The threat she perceives in her surroundings has in turn made the memory itself more volatile. When Adaeze is already on edge — already scanning, already braced — any sudden movement by a colleague reaching across a conference table or a door swinging open unexpectedly floods her with the horror and shame she associates with that night, and the fragments of the crash press forward with renewed force. She has come to believe that strong negative feelings are themselves dangerous signals, that fear or anger means something terrible is imminent, and this belief keeps her nervous system in a state of near-constant readiness. That readiness, paradoxically, makes her more sensitive to the very triggers she fears: a cold glass of water pressed into her hand by a well-meaning intern, the faint smell of something scorched from the building's ventilation system — each one detonates the alarm before she can reason her way around it.

She has also developed a habit of cutting the memory short. When a fragment begins to surface — when she can feel the cold or smell the alcohol approaching in her mind — she pushes it away before it can complete itself, a strategy that has given her brief relief but left the event unprocessed and perpetually close to the surface.

Over the past year, Adaeze has quietly reorganised her professional life around these sensitivities. She no longer attends evening receptions. She sits near exits. She has declined two field assignments that would have required travel by car. Colleagues have noticed her withdrawal, and a junior analyst she mentored for years recently asked if she was all right.

That question, more than anything, brought her to seek help. What she fears most is that she will never again feel safe in the world she has spent her life trying to improve. What she hopes for, with cautious and exhausted honesty, is simply to get through a working day without bracing for a crash that has already happened.
